title: Can You Leave a Puppy Alone for 8 Hours? What Sources Say and What to Do Instead
description: How long can you leave a puppy alone? What the AKC, VCA, Dogs Trust and RSPCA say, why 8 hours is too long for a young puppy, and practical options.
excerpt: What the sources say about leaving a puppy alone, why 8 hours is too long for a young puppy, and what to do if you work full time.
seoTitle: Can You Leave a Puppy Alone for 8 Hours?
imageAlt: PuppyGuido article cover: Can You Leave a Puppy Alone for 8 Hours? What Sources Say and What to Do Instead
coverAlt: Shiba Inu puppy standing up against an indoor door, waiting
html:
For a young puppy, a full 8-hour workday alone is longer than the guidance we found supports. The American Kennel Club suggests about 1 hour for puppies under 10 weeks, rising to roughly 6 hours at 6 months. VCA gives a similar "hours equal months of age" rule, while Dogs Trust and the RSPCA suggest no more than four hours for dogs in general. If you work full time, the realistic fix is to split the day with a break, not to stretch your puppy's limits.

What the sources say

These sources do not agree on every number. We list them side by side so you can see the range.

SourceWhat it says
AKCUnder 10 weeks: 1 hour. 10 to 12 weeks: 2 hours. 3 months: 3 hours. 4 months: 4 hours. 5 months: 5 hours. 6 months: 6 hours. Over 6 months: maximum 6 to 8 hours.
VCA Animal HospitalsGeneral rule: a puppy can be left alone for about as many hours as its age in months, up to 6 months. Its house-training guide says crating for short periods of no more than 3 hours is usually fine.
Humane World for AnimalsPuppies under 6 months should not stay in a crate for more than three or four hours at a time. Its FAQ also gives "age in months plus one hour" for crating.
Dogs Trust (UK)Dogs should not be left alone for more than four hours.
RSPCA (UK)Left for no longer than four hours, depending on the individual dog.
PDSA (UK, crate page)A crate should not be used for longer than three hours at a time, less if the dog is not used to it.

Three things stand out:

  1. Most sources that give puppy numbers land between about 1 and 6 hours, depending on age, and the rules disagree by an hour or so.
  2. The UK charities give a lower flat limit for dogs in general.
  3. None of them says an 8-hour stretch is fine for a young puppy.

Dogs Trust, RSPCA and PDSA are UK organizations. AKC, VCA and Humane World are US. None replaces your own vet's advice about your puppy.

Why the number matters

A puppy who has to wait too long may have accidents, and AKC advises a schedule of bathroom breaks and exercise. AKC says crate time should be no longer than your dog can hold their bladder, and that it should not be all day, every day. PDSA's crate page gives a three-hour limit. VCA says extended periods of confinement are not healthy for animals.

Your options if you work full time

OptionWhat the sources say
Come home at lunchAKC suggests coming home for lunch or hiring someone to do it.
Hire a walker or sitterAKC suggests someone lets the puppy out at least once or twice a day. Humane World suggests a pet sitter or daycare. VCA suggests a friend or pet sitter for absences over 3 hours.
Doggy daycareDogs Trust, Humane World and ASPCA all mention daycare.
Family or friendsAKC and RSPCA suggest friends or family can help, especially in the first days after bringing a puppy home.
Take your dog to workASPCA suggests this if possible, in its guidance on dogs that struggle alone.
Take leave at the start(General guidance) Many owners reduce their hours for the first days or weeks. Not covered in the sources we checked.

For an hour-by-hour plan around these breaks, use our puppy schedule for working owners.

Teach your puppy to be alone, a step at a time

Whatever your hours, a puppy needs to learn to be comfortable alone. Dogs Trust and the RSPCA both recommend building up gradually, starting with very short periods.

The RSPCA describes a ladder you can follow:

  1. Your puppy settles in their bed while you are nearby.
  2. Your puppy stays settled while you move away.
  3. You move further away and for longer.
  4. You leave the room and close the door, then lengthen the time.
  5. Once your puppy is happy, build toward longer periods, up to about an hour.

Repeat each step until your puppy is relaxed before moving on. Dogs Trust adds: start with a few minutes, and if your puppy shows signs of anxiety, shorten the time. There is no source for an exact timeline, so go at your puppy's pace.

Before you leave

  • Exercise and toilet first. RSPCA says to exercise before leaving, and to make sure your dog goes to the toilet before being left alone. PDSA says the same about feeding, exercise, playtime and a bathroom visit.
  • A safe space. Dogs Trust suggests a "den" away from the household bustle. AKC suggests a crate or an exercise pen. VCA suggests a pen or gated area with a pad for absences over 3 hours.
  • Something to do. Dogs Trust suggests a long-lasting treat or food toy, and says leaving a TV or radio on may help. RSPCA suggests a special toy given only when you leave. AKC mentions a white noise machine.
  • Water. Dogs Trust says to make sure your dog has access to water. PDSA says the same for dogs in a crate.
  • Pads. AKC says puppy pads may help owners who cannot come home often, but they can sometimes slow the move to going outside.
  • A calm goodbye (general guidance).

New to crates? See our crate training guide. For rest between breaks, see the puppy nap and sleep schedule.

Signs your puppy is struggling

Dogs Trust lists panting, pacing, yawning when not tired, lip licking, vocalizing, urinating and destructive behavior. RSPCA adds barking, howling, trembling and whining.

  • If your puppy shows these signs, shorten the time apart and go back a step.
  • If it continues, contact your vet. RSPCA says a vet may refer you to a clinical animal behaviourist, and ASPCA recommends ruling out medical issues with your vet.
  • PDSA warns that crates should not be used to manage separation anxiety without professional guidance.

A few common mistakes

  • Treating the maximum as the target. The numbers above are upper limits, not goals.
  • Using a crate for the whole day. See the crate limits above.
  • Skipping the build-up. Going straight to a long absence goes against the gradual approach recommended by Dogs Trust and RSPCA.
  • Punishing accidents (general guidance). Our potty training schedule covers what to do instead.

When to ask a professional

  • Your puppy panics, howls or tries to escape when left
  • Accidents or destruction every time you leave
  • You cannot arrange breaks and are worried about the hours

Your vet is the right first call, and they can refer you to an accredited trainer or behaviourist. This article is general information, not veterinary advice.

Make it manageable

Planning a puppy around a job is a lot. Our free New Puppy Survival Guide is a gentle place to start.

If you want a printable plan, the New Puppy Starter Kit has a 30-day plan, a potty schedule and log, a crate checklist and a first-week checklist.
quick: Sources suggest roughly 1 hour for the youngest puppies, rising to about 6 hours at 6 months (AKC, VCA). Dogs Trust and RSPCA suggest no more than four hours for dogs in general. If you work full time, split the day with a midday break and build up alone time gradually.

faq.q: How long can a 2-month-old puppy be left alone?
faq.a: By AKC's table, under 10 weeks about 1 hour, and 10 to 12 weeks about 2 hours. VCA's age-in-months rule gives about 2 hours at 2 months.

faq.q: Can I leave my puppy alone for 8 hours?
faq.a: Not at a young age, according to these sources. Even AKC's table does not reach 6 hours until about 6 months. Dogs Trust and RSPCA suggest four hours as a limit for dogs generally.

faq.q: How long can a puppy stay in a crate?
faq.a: PDSA says no longer than three hours at a time. Humane World says three to four hours for puppies under 6 months. AKC says crate time should be no longer than your dog can hold their bladder, and not all day.
Dogs Trust and PDSA both say to make sure your dog has access to water.

faq.q: Should I use pads or a playpen?
faq.a: AKC says pads may help owners who cannot return often, but they can slow the move to outdoor toileting. VCA suggests a pen or gated area with a pad for absences over 3 hours. Ask your trainer or vet what suits your puppy.

faq.q: Is it OK to leave a puppy with the TV on?
faq.a: Dogs Trust says it may help. We did not find stronger evidence than that.
